Boeing leaves open possibility of more layoffs amid stalled production plans

The company said cuts are needed as 737 MAX output increases lag, with its 47-jets-a-month target now expected in early 2027.

SEATTLE: When pressed by one of its largest unions, Boeing management declined to say on Thursday (Nov 20) if the company plans on further layoffs after an upcoming round next month. "We asked if December 9 was the only date for (layoff notices) and were told Boeing didn't know," Bryan Corliss, a spokesman for the Society of Engineering Employees in Aerospace, told Reuters. In early November, Boeing announced plans to cut 5 per cent of the company's commercial airplanes division's roughly 50,000 employees through attrition and layoffs . The cuts were needed because it is taking longer than expected for the company to increase output of its 737 MAX jet, its largest moneymaker, the division's CEO Stephanie Pope explained in a memo to employees at the time. Asked about SPEEA's comment, a Boeing spokesperson told Reuters, “We continue to work through an established process to ensure our workforce can support our customer commitments. We are committed to treating everyone with dignity and respect and will communicate details with impacted employees once decisions are finalised.”

The company is trying to increase 737 production rate from 42 jets a month to 47, which it had planned to reach this past summer. Last month, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors that the company now expects to reach that target in early 2027.

Related:

On Thursday, SPEEA told its roughly 17,000 members that Boeing managers told union officials that: "Employment at all Boeing Commercial Airplanes sites is under review, but layoffs won’t necessarily impact all sites. "These will not be across-the-board layoffs , but rather targeted layoffs focused on which work statements are ending or can be ended. "There will be no voluntary layoffs or buy-outs." SPEEA members approved a new four-year contract with the company in early October. Boeing managers told the union that the cuts were not retaliation for the contract, which included a guaranteed 10 per cent wage increase upon ratification, along with annual raises of 4 per cent and the possibility of an additional 2 per cent pay hike based on performance.

Source: Reuters/fs

LONDON: A British man prosecutors said was motivated by extreme right-wing ideology was convicted on Friday (Nov 20) of planning a terrorist attack with petrol bomb s on a hotel housing asylum seekers. Mikka Lee Anderson, 24, was found guilty of targeting the Royal Hotel in Hull, northeast England, including by making Molotov cocktails and conducting reconnaissance. The hotel had previously been the focus of violent anti-migration riots that swept Britain in 2024 after the murder of three young girls in Southport. Anderson denied intending to commit any violent acts, but prosecutors told jurors that Anderson had told an associate of his plan to attack the hotel and "kill as man y of the migrant s who were housed inside it as possible."

Prosecutor Adam Birkby said Anderson was inspired by his belief in white nationalism, spoke admiringly about Adolf Hitler and Nazism and took practical steps towards a violent attack . After a trial at Newcastle Crown Court this month, Anderson was found guilty of preparing an act of terrorism and possessing weapons for terrorist purposes. He will be sentenced next year. Anderson's convictions are the latest for terrorism offences linked to extreme right-wing ideology, after British army chef Mark Broadhurst was jailed last month for possession of a homemade gun and explosives. Broadhurst, 28, had been in a Telegram group with three other men who were jailed last year for planning to carry out a terrorist attack at mosques or synagogues.

TAMPA, Florida: A US judge in Florida on Thursday (Nov 19) declared Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal court charge accusing him of being a child sexual predator. Accepting the findings of a court-appointed forensic psychiatrist, US Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin ruled the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was mentally fit to understand the proceedings against him and to properly assist in his own defence, court records showed. Neither prosecutors nor the defence disputed the findings of the psychiatrist's evaluation, contained in a 15-page report and based in large part on the doctor's in-person interview with Markle in prison last week. Markle was charged on Nov 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question, including two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress, was found in two Los Angeles storage units. Commenting on the case at the time of Markle's arrest on Nov 6 at an assisted-living centre in Florida, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle had "targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions". Griffin's ruling capped a competency proceeding set in motion by the judge after Markle's first court hearing on the day of his arrest. In ordering a psychiatric examination of the defendant, Griffin wrote that she found "reasonable cause" to believe Markle was suffering from some mental deficiency, based in part on his advanced age and "lack of recall" during his first court appearance the day of his arrest. Dr Aime Gerodimos, who conducted the evaluation, wrote in her report that Markle appeared to suffer from a "major neurocognitive disorder," possibly the result of mild vascular disease. She also found he was likely "exaggerating deficits" when asked to recall specifics of the allegations against him. The psychiatrist concluded that Markle "does have sufficient present ability to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him and to assist properly in his defence" - the legal standard for a criminal defendant to be deemed competent.

Related:

CASE ORIGINATED IN PHILIPPINES Markle was first taken into custody at the assisted-living facility where he was residing in Lakeland, Florida, near Tampa. Griffin initially ordered him placed under home confinement on the condition that Markle wear an electronic monitoring device. But days later, the judge revoked the arrangement and ordered him back to jail without bond after Markle cut off his electronic ankle tag with a knife . It remained unclear when Markle would be transferred to federal custody in California, where the case against him was lodged. The judge on Thursday set a preliminary hearing in the case for Dec 1 in Tampa. According to the FBI affidavit, federal agents acting on a search warrant earlier this month seized a large cache of slides, film negatives and books from two storage lockers Markle had rented in Los Angeles since 2008. One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, where Markle previously resided and where authorities initiated an investigation of him last month, the affidavit said. Philippine police said on Wednesday criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country’s Cebu province, where he lived. The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police said. Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies." Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of the allegations against her father. She has said she was "deeply distressed" over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

Source: Reuters/nh

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or Beijing, three people told Reuters. The Treasury Department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb, the people said. The company uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power its AI customer service agent. Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites. It was not immediately clear if the idea was gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a formal rulemaking process if it does move forward.

But its consideration, first reported by Reuters, underscores an emerging push within the administration toward combating the spread of powerful Chinese open weight models, a source of deep concern within the government. Open weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt. The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI. The White House, the Treasury Department and Alibaba did not respond to requests for comment. Airbnb said in a statement that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on US-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved US-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected". The Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing opposes politicising trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests. We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights and interests", it added. The consideration comes as revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy have fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China . They have turned a spotlight on cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

Also read:

China's access to Nvidia chips in doubt as curbs gain traction in US Congress

Nvidia faces deepening scrutiny over China chip ties, CEO affair

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, and perform well enough. But China hawks fear Beijing is using such models - like Moonshot AI's Kimi, DeepSeek or Qwen - to hook US companies so they will become dependent on Chinese AI. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft via distillation of American models. Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool. Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by Michael Kratsios, OSTP director, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale", spurring a State Department-led push to highlight such behavior to foreign counterparts.

Also read:

US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia

China slams new US chip curbs, vows 'necessary measures'

CONGRESSIONAL INVESTIGATION But US officials have stopped short of restricting or taking punitive action against Chinese AI companies. The issue has attracted the attention of Congress. Republican US Representatives Andrew Garbarino of New York and John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chair the House Homeland Security Committee and the House select committee on China, respectively, launched an investigation into American companies' use of Chinese AI this year. They sent letters to Airbnb as well as Anysphere, the maker of the AI coding tool Cursor, whose Composer 2 AI model was built on a version of Kimi. A letter was also sent to DoorDash, whose co-founder said the company routes some tasks in an internal system through Kimi. Moonshot, DoorDash, and SpaceX, which bought Anysphere, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Moolenaar welcomed news of the Trump administration's deliberations. "Disclosure is an important step in managing the potential risks posed by the diffusion of Chinese open-weight models in the United States,” he said in a statement to Reuters, noting that risks remain even if U companies run Chinese AI models on their own infrastructure. Canada-based Thomson Reuters, which owns Reuters, also uses Alibaba's Qwen, according to a TR spokesperson. She noted that the model was "substantially retrained" to align "with our standards for safety, accuracy and neutrality", and runs entirely within the company's own infrastructure. Chinese AI models were the three most popular by token usage in October on OpenRouter, an AI marketplace platform that tracks usage data. Tokens are units of data processed by AI models. Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government itself. Reuters reported in September that a US government website deployed an AI model from China's Alibaba to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model's developer of copying Anthropic's technology. American open-weight models include Meta's Muse Glimmer, Nvidia's Nemotron and Reflection AI's Beam.

Source: Reuters/co
